# Assignments

This chapter collects each week's assignment in one place for easy
reference. New assignments will be added here as the semester progresses.

## Week 1: Software Setup and Final Project Topic Selection

Before our first class session, please install R and RStudio and verify
your installation.

## Software Requirements and Installation Instructions {-}

Before our first class session, please install the following software.
Come to class with everything installed and verified — we'll do a quick
check together, but coming prepared means we can dive into the material
right away.

### R {-}

R is a free software environment for statistical computing and graphics.
Installing or updating R is a separate process from installing or updating
RStudio (below) — you need both.

- **Windows:** Download the latest version at <https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/base/>
- **Mac OS:** Download the latest version at <https://cran.r-project.org/bin/macosx/>
- **Linux:** Follow the instructions for your distribution at <https://cloud.r-project.org/bin/linux/>

### RStudio {-}

RStudio is a free Integrated Development Environment (IDE) for R. Installing
or updating RStudio is separate from installing or updating R.

Download it from <https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/>.

## The RStudio Interface {-}

When you open RStudio, you'll see the window divided into four panes. Each
one serves a different purpose:

**Source (top left)**
This is where you write and edit scripts, RMarkdown documents, and other
files. Code you write here isn't run automatically — you need to send it to
the Console (below) to execute it. Keeping your code in the Source pane,
rather than typing directly into the Console, is what makes your work
reproducible: it's saved, shareable, and can be re-run from start to finish.

**Console (bottom left)**
This is where R actually executes code and shows you the results. You can
type commands directly into the Console, but anything you type there isn't
saved anywhere — so it's best used for quick, one-off checks rather than your
actual analysis.

**Environment / History (top right)**
The Environment tab shows you all the objects (data frames, variables,
functions, etc.) currently loaded in your R session, along with their type
and a preview of their contents. The History tab keeps a running log of every
command you've executed in the Console during your session.

**Files / Plots / Packages / Help (bottom right)**
This pane is multi-purpose. *Files* lets you browse your project's folder
structure. *Plots* displays any graphs or visualizations you create. *Packages*
shows which R packages are installed and lets you load or update them. *Help*
displays documentation when you look up a function.

You can resize any pane by dragging its borders, and rearrange their
positions under **Tools > Global Options > Pane Layout** if you'd prefer a
different arrangement.

### Required R Packages {-}

We'll be using the following R packages throughout the course: `tidyverse`,
`rmarkdown`, `bookdown`, and `renv`. Install them, along with their dependencies, by running the
following in the R console:

```r
install.packages(c("tidyverse",
                    "rmarkdown",
                    "bookdown",
                    "renv"), dependencies = TRUE)
```

### Verifying Your Installation {-}

To confirm everything is working, open RStudio and run the following in
the console:

```r
R.version.string
library(tidyverse)
library(bookdown)
library(renv)
```

If R prints a version number and the `tidyverse` loads without error
messages, you're all set.

### Dataset eligibility criteria

Your dataset must meet the following criteria:

- **Public availability:** The dataset must be publicly accessible — for
  example, from a government agency, public data repository, or a published
  study's supplementary materials. No proprietary, restricted-access, or
  personally identifiable data.
- **Minimum size:** At least **100 rows (observations)** and **10 variables
  (columns)**.
- **Rationale:** A short written explanation (3–5 sentences) of why this
  dataset interests you and what you hope to learn from it.
- **Exploratory questions:** At least 2–3 questions you want to answer using
  this dataset by the end of the course.


### What to submit

Go to Canvas, and submit a screen shot of your R console output for the 
"Week 1" assignment that shows your successful download.

Then in the text box, submit the following:

- A brief description of your dataset, including an overview of how the data were collected, how many observations there are, and how many variables were measured.
- A short written explanation (3–5 sentences) of why this dataset interests you and what you hope to learn from it.
- At least 2–3 questions you want to answer using this dataset by the end of the course.
- A brief description on any data cleaning you anticipate needing to do, based on an initial look at the file.

## Week 2: Project Directory Structure and Git Setup

Now that you've chosen your final project dataset, it's time to set up the
project itself as a properly structured, version-controlled repository.

### What to do

**1. Design your directory structure.**

Based on what we covered in Chapter 1, plan out a folder structure for your
final project. At minimum, your structure should separate raw data,
scripts, and output — but feel free to adapt it to fit your specific
project.

**2. Create the folders locally.**

Make a new folder for your project (name it something descriptive, e.g.
`final-project`), then create your subfolders inside it. You can do this in
Finder/File Explorer, or from the terminal. For example, from inside your
project folder:

```
mkdir data
mkdir data/raw
mkdir data/processed
mkdir scripts
mkdir output
mkdir output/figures
```

(Adjust folder names to match your own planned structure — this is just an
example.)

**3. Turn it into a Git repository.**

Navigate into your project folder in the terminal (recall the drag-and-drop
or Option+right-click tricks from Chapter 2 if you need to find the path),
then run:

```
git init
```

**4. Add a `.gitignore` file.**

Create a new plain-text file named exactly `.gitignore` in your project's
top-level folder (see Chapter 2 for instructions specific to your
operating system). At minimum, include the following:

```
.Rhistory
.Rproj.user/
.DS_Store
```

Add any additional rules relevant to your own project — for example, if
you'll be working with large raw data files you don't want tracked.

**5. Add a README.**

Create a new plain-text file named `README.md` in your project's top-level
folder. At minimum, it should include:

- Your project title and a one-paragraph description of what it's about
- A brief explanation of your folder structure (what lives where)
- A note on your data source (a link or citation)

**6. Make your first commit.**

From inside your project folder, run:

```
git add .
git commit -m "Initial project structure"
```

### What to submit

Submit a short document (PDF or Word) containing:

1. A screenshot showing your folder structure.
2. A brief paragraph (3–5 sentences) explaining your folder structure —
   what each top-level folder is for and why you organized it this way.

## Week 3: Creating a GitHub Repository for Your Project

In Week 2, you created a local Git repository for your final project. This
week, you'll put that repository on GitHub so it's backed up remotely and
ready for collaboration.

### What to do

**1. Create a new repository on GitHub.**

- Go to <https://github.com> and log in.
- Click the **+** icon in the top-right corner and select **New repository**.
- Fill out the repository details:
  - **Repository name:** Use a short, descriptive name for your project
    (e.g., `my-lastname-final-project`)
  - **Description:** One sentence describing your project topic
  - **Visibility:** Choose **Public** (unless your data requires restricted
    access, in which case choose **Private**)
  - **Do NOT** check "Add a README file," "Add .gitignore," or "Choose a
    license" — your local repo already has these files, and we'll connect
    it directly
- Click **Create repository**. GitHub will show you a page with setup
  instructions — keep this page open.

**2. Connect your local repo to GitHub.**

Copy the repository URL from the GitHub page (it will look like
`https://github.com/yourusername/your-repo-name.git`). Then, from inside
your project folder, run the following, replacing `<repo-url>` with the URL
you copied:

```
git remote add origin <repo-url>
git branch -M main
git push -u origin main
```

If prompted for a username and password, enter your GitHub username. For
the password, use a Personal Access Token (PAT) instead of your account
password (see Chapter 3 for a refresher on generating one).

**3. Verify it worked.**

Refresh your repository's page on GitHub and confirm that your project
files — including your `.gitignore` and `README.md` — appear there.

### What to submit

Submit the following:

1. A screenshot of your repository's GitHub page showing your files.
2. The URL to your GitHub repository.

## Week 4: Designing a Tidy Spreadsheet for a Bear Research Case Study

This week, you'll apply the tidy data principles from Chapter 4 to a new
scenario — not your own final project dataset, but a case study describing
a black bear research project. Real field data collection is often
described informally, in field notes or verbal summaries, rather than
handed to you as a ready-made spreadsheet. Your job is to translate a
messy, informal description of a research project into a properly
structured, tidy spreadsheet design.

### The case study

A research team is studying a black bear population in a mountainous study
area. Here's how they describe their data collection process:

> "We trap bears using culvert traps and snares placed at a handful of
> fixed trap sites scattered across the study area. Every time we catch a
> bear — whether it's the first time or a recapture — we record the date,
> which trap site it was caught at, and the bear's ID (new bears get a new
> ID; if we recognize an ear tag from a previous capture, we reuse that
> ID). At first capture, we record the bear's sex. Every time we handle a
> bear, whether it's a new capture or a recapture, we take its weight and
> body length, and we note its age class (cub, yearling, or adult). Over
> the course of the study, we catch dozens of different bears, some of
> them multiple times, at several different trap sites, across several
> field seasons."

### What to do

**1. Identify the variables and observations.**

Read through the case study carefully. For each piece of information being
collected, ask: what is being measured (a variable)? Then think about what
a single row in your table should represent — one bear? One capture event?
Be careful here: a bear that's caught three times shouldn't be squeezed
into a single row, since its weight, length, age class, trap site, and
date are all different at each capture.

**2. Design your table.**

Sketch out the column headers your table needs, keeping in mind that the
same bear ID will appear on more than one row (once per capture), while
other information (like sex) stays the same across all of that bear's
rows. This is expected and fine — it's how a single tidy table
accommodates repeated measurements on the same individual.

**3. Build the actual spreadsheet template.**

In Excel or Google Sheets, create your table with only column headers
filled in — you don't need to invent or enter any actual data rows. Column
headers should be computer-readable (following the naming conventions from
Chapter 1: no spaces, no special characters, consistent capitalization).

Pay close attention to the tidy data pitfalls from Chapter 4 as you design
your headers: don't cram two variables into one column (like age class and
sex), don't let a single cell need to hold more than one value, and make
sure your table's unit of observation is consistent row to row.

**4. Write a short justification.**

In a separate document (or as a second tab/sheet), briefly explain:

- What a single row in your table represents.
- At least one specific design decision where the case study's informal
  description could have easily led to an un-tidy spreadsheet, and how
  your design avoids that trap.

### What to submit

Submit the following to Canvas:

1. Your spreadsheet file (.xlsx or a link to a Google Sheet with sharing
   enabled), containing only column headers filled in.
2. Your written justification (1 paragraph is sufficient).

## Week 5 Assignment: Querying the Bird Nest Box Database

This assignment uses a new practice database, `birds.sqlite`, covering a
nest box study with three habitat types (farmland, residential, forest).
Adults are banded, GPS-tagged, and have blood hormone samples and gut
microbiome samples taken. Hatchlings are banded and sexed at hatch,
measured regularly until fledging, and GPS-tagged just before fledging.

Unlike the in-class activity in Chapter 6, this time you're given five
complete, working queries. Your job isn't to write SQL from scratch, it's
to run each query, understand what it's doing, and interpret what the
result actually tells you biologically. This is just as important a skill
as writing queries in the first place: in practice, you'll often be
reading and adapting someone else's SQL (a labmate's, a collaborator's,
your own from six months ago) far more often than starting from a blank
page.

### Getting the data

`birds.sqlite` lives in the `data/` folder of the course repository,
alongside `frogs.sqlite`. If you already cloned the repo back in Chapter
6, just make sure you're up to date:

### Setup

```{r, eval=FALSE}
library(DBI)

con <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), "data/birds.sqlite")
dbListTables(con)
```

### Query 1: Do males and females differ in nest attendance during incubation?

Neither `nests` nor `gps_fixes` has a column that says "this bird was
incubating right now." Instead, we infer it: a GPS fix very close to the
nest box's coordinates (within a small distance threshold) during the
incubation period (before the eggs hatch) is treated as "at the nest."
Everything else counts as "away." For the purposes of this example, the 
researchers set a distance threshold of 0.003 degrees from the nest box to 
determine at the nest vs. away.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT
    b.sex,
    SUM(CASE WHEN (ABS(g.lat - nb.latitude) + ABS(g.lon - nb.longitude)) < 0.003
             THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS nest_fixes,
    COUNT(*) AS total_fixes,
    ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN (ABS(g.lat - nb.latitude) + ABS(g.lon - nb.longitude)) < 0.003
                           THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS pct_at_nest
  FROM gps_fixes g
  JOIN deployments d ON g.tracker_id = d.tracker_id
  JOIN birds b ON d.bird_id = b.bird_id
  JOIN nests n ON b.bird_id IN (n.female_id, n.male_id)
  JOIN nest_boxes nb ON n.box_id = nb.box_id
  WHERE g.timestamp <= n.hatch_date
    AND b.entry_stage != 'hatchling'
  GROUP BY b.sex;
")
```

**Question:** Based on the output, do males or females spend more time at
the nest during incubation? Does this match what you'd expect
biologically, or does it surprise you? 

**Question:** The distance threshold, `0.003` degrees, is a simplification,
real studies would use a proper distance calculation and a threshold
chosen based on GPS accuracy and nest box spacing.

Write a query that finds the distance between every pair of nest boxes,
and identifies the two closest boxes and how far apart they are. (Hint:
this requires joining the `nest_boxes` table to itself, a **self-join**,
something we haven't explicitly covered yet. You can join a table to
itself just like any other join, just give each copy a different alias,
e.g. `FROM nest_boxes a JOIN nest_boxes b ON a.box_id < b.box_id`, then
compute a distance between `a`'s and `b`'s coordinates. The `<` in the
`ON` clause, rather than `!=`, avoids getting every pair twice and avoids
comparing a box to itself.)

<!--
ANSWER KEY (not visible in rendered output)

SELECT
  a.box_id AS box_a,
  b.box_id AS box_b,
  ROUND(ABS(a.latitude - b.latitude) + ABS(a.longitude - b.longitude), 4) AS distance
FROM nest_boxes a
JOIN nest_boxes b ON a.box_id < b.box_id
ORDER BY distance ASC
LIMIT 5;

Closest pair: boxes 1 and 2, distance 0.006 (only 2x the 0.003 threshold).
-->

Once you have that result, answer: is the `0.003` threshold safely
smaller than the distance between the closest two boxes, or is it cutting
it close? What would happen to a GPS fix that happened to fall roughly
halfway between those two closest boxes, and why might that be a problem
for this specific pair, even if it's not a problem for most other box
pairs in the dataset?

### Query 2: Are some GPS tracker models more prone to being lost?

Just like "at the nest," "lost" isn't a column anywhere in this database.
A tracker is inferred to be lost when its deployment has no
`retrieved_date`, meaning it was never brought back in.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT
    t.tracker_model,
    COUNT(*) AS n_deployments,
    SUM(CASE WHEN d.retrieved_date IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS n_lost,
    ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN d.retrieved_date IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
          / COUNT(*), 1) AS pct_lost
  FROM deployments d
  JOIN trackers t ON d.tracker_id = t.tracker_id
  GROUP BY t.tracker_model
  ORDER BY pct_lost DESC;
")
```

**Question:** Which tracker model has the highest loss rate? Given this
result, what would you recommend to the research team about which
tracker model to use going forward, and what else would you want to know
before making that call (e.g., cost, weight, battery life)?

**Question:** This query has one specific detail that's easy to overlook
but important for getting a correct result: the `100.0` (written as
`100.0`, not just `100`) in the `ROUND(100.0 * SUM(...) / COUNT(*), 1)`
line.

Which single line in the query is this, and what job is it doing? (Hint:
think about how SQLite handles division when both numbers involved are
whole numbers, versus when one of them has a decimal point.)

Try it yourself: change `100.0` to plain `100` in your query, rerun it,
and compare the `pct_lost` column to your original result. What changes,
and why? Which tracker model's row shows the clearest difference between
the two versions, and what does that tell you about when this kind of
mistake would be most likely to go unnoticed?

### Query 3: Does hatchling growth differ by habitat type?

This compares hatchling mass around day 15 of life (just before
fledging) across the three habitat types nest boxes are placed in.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT
    nb.location_type,
    ROUND(AVG(m.mass_g), 1) AS avg_mass_g,
    COUNT(*) AS n_records
  FROM morphometrics m
  JOIN birds b ON m.bird_id = b.bird_id
  JOIN nests n ON b.natal_nest_id = n.nest_id
  JOIN nest_boxes nb ON n.box_id = nb.box_id
  WHERE b.entry_stage = 'hatchling'
    AND julianday(m.measurement_date) - julianday(n.hatch_date) BETWEEN 13 AND 17
  GROUP BY nb.location_type
  ORDER BY avg_mass_g DESC;
")
```

**Question:** How much difference is there between habitat types? Given
the `n_records` column, do you think this dataset has enough
observations to draw a confident conclusion either way?

**Question:** This query needs to figure out how old each hatchling was,
in days, at the time of each measurement, using two date columns:
`m.measurement_date` and `n.hatch_date`. Which line does this, and what
does the `julianday()` function do?

Try running just this piece on its own to see what it returns:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT measurement_date, julianday(measurement_date)
  FROM morphometrics
  LIMIT 5;
")
```

Dates in this database are stored as plain text (e.g., `'2023-05-03'`),
not as a special date type. Why can't you just subtract two date strings
directly, the way you might subtract two numbers? What would
`'2023-05-20' - '2023-05-03'` even mean to SQLite, and why does wrapping
each one in `julianday()` first solve that problem?

One more thing to notice: the query also has a `WHERE b.entry_stage =
'hatchling'` line. Given that the `JOIN` to `nests` uses
`b.natal_nest_id = n.nest_id`, and only hatchlings have a non-`NULL`
`natal_nest_id` (adults don't), is that `WHERE` line actually doing
anything here, or is it redundant? Explain your reasoning.

### Query 4: Does parent stress hormone level differ by habitat type?

Corticosterone is the primary stress hormone in birds, and the researchers 
hypothesize that bird parents in urban environments would show higher stress
levels than bird parents in forests.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT
    nb.location_type,
    ROUND(AVG(h.corticosterone), 2) AS avg_cort,
    COUNT(*) AS n_samples
  FROM hormones h
  JOIN birds b ON h.bird_id = b.bird_id
  JOIN nests n ON b.bird_id IN (n.female_id, n.male_id)
  JOIN nest_boxes nb ON n.box_id = nb.box_id
  GROUP BY nb.location_type
  ORDER BY avg_cort DESC;
")
```

**Question:** Which habitat type shows the highest average
corticosterone? Propose one biological explanation for why that habitat
might be more stressful for a nesting bird. Given the sample sizes shown,
how confident are you in this pattern?

**Question:** Look at the `JOIN` line connecting `birds` to `nests`:

```
JOIN nests n ON b.bird_id IN (n.female_id, n.male_id)
```

This looks a little different from the joins we've used so far, it uses `IN` instead of a plain `=`. Why can't this line just say `ON b.bird_id = n.female_id`? What would that simpler version miss, and why does `IN (n.female_id, n.male_id)` fix it?

### Query 5: Does gut microbiome richness differ between adults and hatchlings?

This counts the number of distinct OTUs (a proxy for microbial diversity)
detected per bird, then compares the average across adults and
hatchlings.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT
    b.entry_stage,
    ROUND(AVG(otu_count), 1) AS avg_otus_per_bird
  FROM (
    SELECT bird_id, COUNT(DISTINCT otu_id) AS otu_count
    FROM otu_reads
    GROUP BY bird_id
  ) sub
  JOIN birds b ON sub.bird_id = b.bird_id
  GROUP BY b.entry_stage;
")
```

**Question:** This query uses a subquery, a query nested inside another
query (the inner `SELECT` runs first, and the outer query treats its
result like a table). In your own words, explain what the inner subquery
computes, and why it needs to run before the outer `GROUP BY` can work.
Then interpret the result: do adults or hatchlings show higher microbial
richness, and can you think of a biological reason that might be true?

**Question:** Look at the inner subquery:

```
SELECT bird_id, COUNT(DISTINCT otu_id) AS otu_count
FROM otu_reads
GROUP BY bird_id
```

Try removing `GROUP BY bird_id` from just this inner piece, and run the whole query again. What happens to the result? Why does dropping this one line break the entire comparison between adults and hatchlings, even though the outer query still has its own `GROUP BY b.entry_stage` line? What is `GROUP BY bird_id` actually accomplishing here that the outer `GROUP BY` can't do on its own?

### What to submit

Submit an RMarkdown document (or plain R script) with all five queries,
their output, and your written answer to each question.

## Week 6: Design Your Final Project Database Structure

Now that you've worked through relational databases (Chapter 5), SQL
(Chapter 6), and building a database from CSVs in R (Chapter 7), it's
time to apply all of that to your own final project. This week, you'll
design the table structure your project's data would actually need,
without building the database itself yet.

### What to do

**1. Revisit your raw data.**

Go back to your Week 1 proposal: your dataset, your rationale, and your
exploratory questions. Keep these in mind as you design, since your
table structure should support the questions you actually want to ask.

Consider how you received your data. Did you collect all your data yourself? 
If so, maybe you already entered your data in a tidy format. But it's ok if you
didn't, because now you know how to do that for your next project. And if you 
are using data that someone else collected, they might not have given you
tidy data either. Finally, sometimes we use data from different sources. We 
may collect biological data ourselves or with a research group, but we may then
obtain additional data from other public sources. Long term climate data, land cover
land use data, hydrologic data, and other similar data are common data sources
in ecosystem science used to supplement what you actually collected. And some of 
that supplemental data you obtain may not be tidy.

All these raw files will go in your data/raw subfolder, and part of your work for the
final project will be process all these different data sources and make them
tidy so that all the datasets can talk to each other, and save them in your
data/processed subfolder.

**2. Decide how many processed data tables you need.**

Your processed data tables will the ones you actually use to analyze and visualize your data. 
Using the principles from Chapter 5, work through whether your data belongs in one table or several:

- What is the sampling unit (or units) in your data? A single
  consistent unit usually means a single table is enough. Multiple
  distinct units (e.g., a site, and repeated visits to that site) often
  means multiple tables.
- Is there a mix of static information (recorded once) and dynamic
  information (recorded repeatedly)? If so, consider splitting them,
  the same logic behind separating a frog's sex from its repeated
  weight measurements.
- Does every column hold one atomic value? If you find yourself wanting
  to cram a list into a single cell, that's usually a sign you need an
  additional table (a junction table, if the relationship is many to
  many, as in our diet_asvs / diet_asv_reads example).

A single table is a completely acceptable answer here, if that's what
your data actually calls for. What matters is that you can justify the
decision using these principles, not that you force complexity your
project doesn't need.

**3. Map out each raw and processed data table.**

For every table your design requires, write out:

- The table name
- Every column header, with its data type (text, integer, float, date,
  boolean)
- Which column is the primary key (if present, your raw data may not have them yet)
- Any foreign keys, and which table and column each one references (if present, 
your raw data may not have them yet)

**4. If you have more than one table, explain the relationships.**

For each pair of related tables, state whether the relationship is one
to many or many to many, and briefly explain why. If it's many to many,
identify the junction table that handles it.

**5. Draw a diagram that visualizes these relationships.**

Using PowerPoint, Google Slides, or a similar tool, draw a diagram of
your table structure, following the same style as the diagrams in
Chapters 5 through 7:

- One box (or text box) per table, with the table name at the top.
- Note if you the table is "raw" or "processed" data
- List every column inside its box, and mark the primary key (e.g.,
  underline it, or add "(PK)" next to it) and any foreign keys (add
  "(FK)" next to them).
- Draw a line or arrow connecting each pair of related tables, from the
  primary key in one table to the matching foreign key in the other.
- Label each connecting line as "1 to many" or "many to many," matching
  the relationships you identified in step 4.

If you have a single table, you don't need any connecting lines, just
one box showing its columns.

### What to submit

Submit a short document (PDF, Word, or a rendered RMarkdown file)
containing:

1. Your diagram (a PowerPoint or Google Slides screenshot/export is
   fine, it doesn't need to be a separate file).
2. Your table map in writing: every table, its columns and data types,
   its primary key, and any foreign keys (this can be redundant with
   your diagram, that's fine, the written version should be
   detailed enough to actually build the database from later).
3. A short paragraph (3-5 sentences) explaining your reasoning: why this
   many tables, and how they relate to each other (or, if you landed on
   a single table, why that's the right call for your data).

## Week 7: Build Your Final Project Database

Last week, you designed the tables your final project needs. This week, you'll build them. As Chapter 5 explained, a database is a set of related tables, and you don't need SQL to have one. For your project, it 
is likely far easier to use use a set of related .csv files, so that is what use instead.

### Before you start

You'll need:

- Your Week 6 table map and diagram.
- Your final project repository from Weeks 2 and 3, on your computer, with your raw data file or files saved in `data/raw/` and left unedited (Chapter 1: never edit raw data by hand).

Your raw data should be saved as CSV files, which is what most public data portals provide. If yours are Excel files, save a CSV copy of each sheet you need into `data/raw/` and keep the original Excel files too.

**1. Save your tables in the data/raw folder in your repo.**

Make sure you save your data as .csv files, that file names are computer readable, that all column names within each file are computer readable, and that all your file and column names follow the conventions you set in your week 6 assignment. At this point, its ok if your raw data isn't tidy, and if they don't have primary keys and foreign keys yet.  We can add those to the processed data later.

**2. Commit and push.**

Your processed CSV files are plain text, they're small, and they let anyone see your tables on GitHub without running anything, so commit them. (If one of your files is very large, tens of megabytes, add it to `.gitignore` and tell the instructor.) 

### What to submit

Submit the link to your final project repository on GitHub.

## Week 8: Describe Your Final Project in RMarkdown

This week, you'll write the first draft of the RMarkdown document that will become your final project report. It won't have any data wrangling or visualization code yet, because we haven't covered those. But it will have everything that doesn't depend on them: the front matter, an overview of your project, its folder structure, and a description of every raw data file you have so far. You'll keep adding to this same file for the rest of the semester, so it's worth getting the foundations right now.

### Before you start

You'll need:

- Your final project repository from Weeks 2 and 3, with your raw data file or files saved in `data/raw/`.
- Your Week 1 proposal: your description of the dataset, your rationale, and your exploratory questions. You'll reuse most of that text.
- For each raw data file, where it came from: a URL or DOI, the date you downloaded it, and its license or terms of use. If you don't remember these, look them up now. Every raw file needs them.

When you knit a document, R works from the folder the `.Rmd` file is in (Chapter 8), so with the file at the top level, paths like `data/raw/my-file.csv` work.

**2. Replace the starter content with the template.**

The template has the parts you learned in Chapter 8: a YAML header, a setup chunk, headers, a table, code chunks, and inline code. A few things in it are worth knowing before you start:

- The date in the header is inline code that fills in today's date each time you knit, so you never have to update it.
- The `setup` chunk at the top has `include=FALSE`, so it doesn't appear in your knitted document. It tells every other chunk to show its code along with its output.
- The `raw-file-list` chunk lists whatever is in `data/raw/` each time you knit, so the list can never be out of date. There is nothing in it to edit.
- `knitr::kable()` turns a data frame into a formatted table.

**3. Fill in the front matter and the introduction.**

**4. Describe your project organization.**

**5. Present your raw data files.**

Do this for each file in `data/raw/`. Start with the "File 1" subsection of the template:

2. Replace the italic paragraph with a description of the file: how the data were collected, what time period and place they cover, and what one row represents.
3. In the first chunk, replace `your-file-name.csv` with your file's name. You can also give the data frame a more meaningful name than `file1`, but if you do, change it everywhere it appears in this subsection, including in the two pieces of inline code.
4. Fill in the data dictionary with one row for each variable (column) in the file, using the exact column names from the file. If a file has more than about 20 variables, document the 10 most important ones and say that you did.

For each additional file, copy everything from the `## File 1` heading down to the end of its data dictionary, paste it below, and make the same changes. Each copy needs its own data frame name (for example `file2`) and its own chunk labels (for example `read-file-2`, `head-file-2`, and `str-file-2`). Two chunks can't share a label.

Two special cases:

- If a raw file isn't a CSV (an Excel workbook, for example), still describe it in the same way, but leave out the chunks that read it. You'll learn to read other formats later in the course.
- If your data came as several files with identical columns (one per year, for example), you can describe them together in one subsection. Say what the files have in common and how they differ, and read just one of them as an example.

**6. Describe your planned workflow.**

Under Data cleaning, Visualization, and Analysis, write 2 or 3 sentences about what you plan to do. For the cleaning, use what you noticed in your raw files above, and your notes from Week 1 on the cleaning you anticipated. You'll write the code in later weeks. Then fill in the References section with the citation for each data source.

**7. Knit and check.**

Click **Knit** at the top of the editor. Fix any errors (see below), then read through the HTML document that opens, and check that:

- the table of contents is on the left, and the date is today's date;
- the file list shows every file in `data/raw/`;
- every raw file has its source details, description, first few rows, column types, and data dictionary;
- the numbers of rows and columns in the text match what you expect;
- no italic placeholder text is left anywhere.

**8. Commit and push.**

In a terminal inside your project folder, run the following. The knitted `.html` file is regenerated every time you knit, so you don't need to commit it, but it does no harm if you do.

```
git add .
git commit -m "Add first draft of final project report"
git push
```

Then open your repository on GitHub and confirm that `final-project.Rmd` is there.

### If something goes wrong

When knitting fails, R tells you where. Look for the words `Quitting from` followed by the line numbers and the label of the chunk that failed. The most likely problems:

- **`cannot open the connection`, with a warning that says `cannot open file 'data/raw/...': No such file or directory`.** The file name in your `read.csv()` line is still the placeholder, or has a typo (capital letters matter), or `final-project.Rmd` isn't in the top-level folder of your project.
- **`Duplicate chunk label 'read-file-1'`.** You copied a file's subsection without changing its chunk labels. Give every chunk its own label.
- **`object 'file1' not found`.** You renamed the data frame in one place but not in the others. Look at the chunks and the inline code below the one that reads the file.
- **`Scanner error: mapping values are not allowed in this context`.** There is a mistake in the YAML header at the top. Check that each indented line is indented with spaces (never tabs) and lines up like the template.
- **A table appears as plain text with `|` characters.** A table needs a blank line before it, and a line of dashes under its header row.

### What to submit

Submit the following:

1. The link to your final project repository on GitHub, with `final-project.Rmd` pushed.
2. Your knitted HTML file, `final-project.html`, uploaded to Canvas.

## Week 9: Publish Your Final Project Report with GitHub Pages

Last week, you wrote the first draft of your final project report as an RMarkdown file. This week, you'll publish it as a website, so that anyone with a link can read it. You'll do it the way Chapter 9 did: instead of knitting the report yourself and uploading the result, you'll set up a GitHub Actions workflow that knits `final-project.Rmd` for you every time you push a change, and publishes the result with GitHub Pages. From then on, your website always matches your repository, and it will keep updating as you add data cleaning and visualization over the coming weeks.

### Before you start

You'll need:

- Your final project repository, with `final-project.Rmd` saved in its top-level folder and pushed to GitHub (Week 8).
- A report that knits without errors on your own computer. If it doesn't, fix that first, because it won't knit on GitHub either.

### What to do

**1. Check that GitHub has everything your report needs.**

The workflow runs on a fresh computer that can only see the files in your repository. Open your repository on GitHub, and confirm that:

- `final-project.Rmd` is at the top level, and
- the `data/raw/` folder is there, with every raw data file that your report reads.

If a raw data file is missing, Git may be ignoring it. In a terminal inside your project folder, run the following (with your file's name), which prints the line of `.gitignore` responsible. Fix that line, then `git add`, commit, and push the file.

```
git check-ignore -v data/raw/my-file.csv
```

Next, look beside your repository's name. It says **Public** or **Private**. GitHub Pages needs a public repository on a free account. If yours says Private, go to **Settings**, scroll to the **Danger Zone** at the bottom, and choose to change the repository's visibility to public. Everything in the repository becomes public, which is fine for a project built on a public dataset.

**2. Add the workflow file.**

On your repository's page on GitHub, click **Add file**, then **Create new file**. In the box for the file name, type `.github/workflows/publish.yml`. (Typing each slash starts a new folder, so after you type `.github/` you'll see it turn into a folder.) Paste the following into the large text box, and click **Commit changes...**, then **Commit changes** again to save it directly to the `main` branch.

```yaml
name: Render and deploy report

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write

concurrency:
  group: "pages"
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2
        with:
          r-version: 'release'

      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-pandoc@v2

      - name: Install R package dependencies
        run: |
          install.packages(c("rmarkdown", "knitr"))
        shell: Rscript {0}

      - name: Render report
        run: |
          rmarkdown::render("final-project.Rmd", output_file = "index.html", output_dir = "docs")
        shell: Rscript {0}

      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v3
        with:
          path: docs

  deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    steps:
      - id: deployment
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v4
```

This is the same workflow as in Chapter 9, with two differences. It renders your single report with `rmarkdown::render()` instead of building a whole book, and it saves the result as `docs/index.html`, which is what a website's front page is called. It also names `ubuntu-24.04` rather than `ubuntu-latest`. GitHub is gradually moving `ubuntu-latest` to a newer version of Ubuntu until November 19, and naming a version keeps your build on the one this assignment was tested on.

The moment you save the file, the workflow starts. Its `deploy` job will fail, which is expected, and the next step fixes it.

**3. Turn on GitHub Pages.**

Go to **Settings**, then **Pages**. Under **Build and deployment**, set **Source** to **GitHub Actions**. Then go to the **Actions** tab, click the run that has the red X, click **Re-run jobs** at the top right, and choose **Re-run failed jobs**. When both jobs show a green check, your site is live. Its address is `https://YOUR-USERNAME.github.io/YOUR-REPOSITORY/`, using your GitHub username and your repository's name. Open it.

**4. Compare the website with your report.**

Your website should look like the HTML file you get when you knit the report on your own computer: the table of contents, every section, and the data tables. Click through it, and check that no `REPLACE` placeholder text is left.

**5. Bring the workflow file to your computer.**

You created the workflow file on GitHub's website, so your computer doesn't have it yet. In a terminal inside your project folder, run the following. Everything on your computer should be pushed first, so that `git status` says `nothing to commit`. If you skip this step, your next push will be rejected.

```
git status
git pull
```

**6. Add the website address, and watch the site update.**

In `final-project.Rmd`, in the Project Organization section, add this sentence right after the sentence that links to your GitHub repository, using your own username and repository name:

```markdown
The report is published at <https://YOUR-USERNAME.github.io/YOUR-REPOSITORY/>
```

Add the same line to your repository's `README.md`. Then save both files, and run the following in your terminal:

```
git add .
git commit -m "Add the website address"
git push
```

Go to the **Actions** tab and watch the new run. When it finishes, refresh your website, and the new sentence should appear.

**7. Keep it building as you add code.**

Over the coming weeks, you'll add code to your report. The workflow can only use what you've given it, so two things now matter. Every data file your code reads has to be pushed to your repository. And every R package your code uses has to be in the workflow's install line. Right now it installs only `rmarkdown` and `knitr`. When you use another package, such as `tidyverse`, open `.github/workflows/publish.yml` on GitHub, click the pencil icon, and change that line to include it, for example:

```
install.packages(c("rmarkdown", "knitr", "tidyverse"))
```

If a build fails, open the failed run, click the job, expand the step with the red X, and read the end of its log, as in Chapter 9's "How to read a failed run."

### If something goes wrong

- **No run appears in the Actions tab, or the tab shows "Get started with GitHub Actions".** GitHub didn't find the workflow file. Open `.github/workflows/publish.yml` in your repository and check that the path is spelled exactly like that. If the workflow is listed but never runs, check that your branch is called `main`, because the workflow only starts when you push to `main`.
- **`Render report` fails with `cannot open the connection`, with a warning that says `cannot open file 'data/raw/...'`.** The report reads a file that isn't in your repository, or whose name or capital letters don't match. See step 1.
- **`Render report` fails with `there is no package called '...'`.** Add the package to the install line of the workflow, as in step 7.
- **`Render report` fails and shows `Quitting from lines ...`.** Those line numbers and the label after them tell you which chunk of `final-project.Rmd` failed.
- **`deploy` fails with `Failed to create deployment (status: 404)` and `Ensure GitHub Pages has been enabled`.** GitHub Pages isn't switched on yet. Do step 3, then re-run the failed jobs.
- **`git push` is rejected with `(fetch first)`.** GitHub has a commit that your computer doesn't, probably the workflow file. Run `git pull`, then push again.
- **The website shows an old version.** Check that the latest run in the **Actions** tab has a green check, wait a minute, and refresh.

### What to submit

Submit the following:

1. The address of your live website.
2. The link to your final project repository on GitHub.

To grade, open the student's website and check that it matches the report from Week 8: the table of contents, the overview and questions, the project organization, every raw data file with its description and data dictionary, and no REPLACE text. Then open the repository and check that .github/workflows/publish.yml is there, that the latest run in the Actions tab is green, and that the website address appears in the report and in the README.

The website is built from final-project.Rmd by the workflow, so the knitted HTML does not need to be committed.

## Week 10: Coding with an AI Assistant

This week, you'll practice the R you've learned in the first three episodes of the Data Carpentry lesson (introduction to R and RStudio, data visualization with ggplot2, and exploring and understanding data). You'll also practice using an AI assistant to write code, as many scientists now do. The lesson recommends avoiding generative AI while you're learning the basics, because you need those skills to judge what an assistant gives you. This assignment comes after you've done that work yourself, and it's about those skills: asking clearly, checking an answer against the data, understanding every line, and changing it. The assistant writes the first draft. Everything else is your job.

### How the assignment works

You'll hand in one RMarkdown document, and you'll build it up as you work. In step 4 you'll create it from a template with six parts. After that, each step tells you which part to fill in next:

| Step | What you do | Part of your document |
|------|-------------|-----------------------|
| 1 to 3 | Look at the data, write your prompt, and get the script from the assistant | None yet. You'll paste these into your document in step 4. |
| 4 | Paste in your prompt and the assistant's code, and run it | Parts 1 and 2 |
| 5 | Check the assistant's work | Part 3 |
| 6 | Explain the code in your own words | Part 4 |
| 7 | Change the code and predict the result | Part 5 |
| 8 | Reflect | Part 6 |
| 9 | Knit the document and submit it | The whole document |

### Ground rules

- Use an AI assistant for Part 2 only: to write the script, and to help with any error messages. You write Parts 3 to 6 yourself, using the lesson, R's help pages (`?`), and web searches.
- Keep a record. Your document will contain the name of the assistant, the date, your prompt, and every error message you pasted back to it.
- Be ready to explain any line of your script in class.
- Any assistant will do, including free ones.
- The lesson describes real concerns about generative AI: its reliability, its energy and water use, and how its models were trained. You can read them in its [Generative AI Help section](https://datacarpentry.github.io/R-ecology-lesson/how-r-thinks-about-data.html#generative-ai-help). You'll think about them in your reflection.

### Before you start

You'll need:

- Episodes 1 to 3 of the lesson completed, with R, RStudio, and the `tidyverse` and `ratdat` packages installed.
- An AI assistant to use.

### What to do

**1. Look at the data yourself first.**

An assistant doesn't know your data, so unless you tell it, it will guess. In the RStudio Console, run the following, and read the help page that appears:

```
library(ratdat)
names(complete_old)
?complete_old
```

**2. Write your prompt.**

An assistant doesn't know your data or your lesson, so your prompt has to tell it everything it needs. Your prompt has four parts:

1. **Who you are and what you're using.** Write this yourself, in a sentence or two. Say that you're learning R, and that you're using the `tidyverse` and `ratdat` packages.
2. **The data.** Write this yourself. Give the name of the data frame, `complete_old`, and say that it's available as soon as `ratdat` is loaded, so no file should be read. List the column names (copy them from the output of `names(complete_old)` in step 1), and add anything you know about them, such as units or missing values.
3. **The tasks.** Paste in the six tasks below.
4. **What to use and what to return.** Paste in the paragraph below. It asks for code only, because explaining the code is your job in Part 4, and it limits the assistant to the functions you've met, so that you can follow what it writes.

To see the difference this makes, here are three prompts for a task that isn't one of yours, a histogram of weight. First, a prompt that leaves the assistant guessing:

```
Write R code to explore the rodent data and make some plots.
```

It doesn't say which data, which packages, or which kind of plot, so the assistant has to guess, and it may guess a file to read or columns that don't exist. A better prompt:

```
I'm using R with the tidyverse and ratdat packages. Make a histogram of weight from the complete_old data frame.
```

This names the packages, the data frame, and the task, but it doesn't list the columns, say anything about missing values or labels, or say what to leave out. The answer may read a file, use functions you haven't met, or come with a long explanation. And here is the kind of prompt we're looking for:

```
I'm learning R, using the tidyverse and ratdat packages. The data frame complete_old is already available once ratdat is loaded, so please don't read any file. Its columns are: record_id, month, day, year, plot_id, species_id, sex, hindfoot_length, weight, genus, species, taxa, plot_type. Weight is in grams, and it has missing values.

Task: make a histogram of weight with ggplot2. Give it a title, and an x axis label that includes the units. Save it as weight_histogram.png in the working directory.

Use only library(), ggplot2 functions, and ggsave(). Do not use pipes or functions such as filter() or mutate(). Give me only the R code, in one block, with a comment before each step. Do not explain it. It must run without errors.
```

Its first paragraph is Parts 1 and 2: who the writer is, what they're using, the data frame, the columns, and what is known about them. Its second paragraph is Part 3, a single task described precisely. Its third paragraph is Part 4. Notice how exactly the task says what the plot should have.

Now it's your turn. Here are your six tasks, for Part 3:

```
Task 1: Load the tidyverse and ratdat packages.

Task 2: Explore the complete_old data frame: show its class, its first 10 rows, its structure, and a summary of every column.

Task 3: Show the minimum of the weight column, first without handling missing values and then with the missing values removed. Then calculate the 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles of weight and of hindfoot_length.

Task 4: Create three vectors by hand: a numeric vector with one missing value, a character vector, and a logical vector. Print the class of each. Then combine a number, a logical value, and a character string into one vector, and print the result and its class.

Task 5: Create a factor from the sex column, and print its levels.

Task 6: Make four plots with ggplot2.
(a) A scatterplot of hindfoot_length (y axis) against weight (x axis), with transparent points.
(b) The same scatterplot, with points colored by plot_type and a colorblind-friendly color scale.
(c) A boxplot of hindfoot_length for each plot_type, with jittered points behind the boxes, no fill on the boxes, and no separate outlier points.
(d) A final version of plot (c) with a black-and-white theme, a title, axis labels that include the units (hindfoot length is in millimeters), no legend, and one panel for each value of sex, stacked in a single column. Save this plot as a PNG file called hindfoot_by_plot_type.png in the working directory.
```

And here is the paragraph for Part 4:

```
Use only these functions: library(), class(), head(), str(), summary(), min(), quantile(), c(), factor(), levels(), and functions from ggplot2. Do not use filter(), select(), mutate(), group_by(), summarize(), or pipes.

Give me only the R code, in one block, with a comment before each task such as # Task 1. Do not explain the code. It must run from top to bottom without errors.
```

Put the four parts together in this order, with a blank line between them:

```
[Part 1: write this yourself. One or two sentences about what you are using.]
```

### If something goes wrong

- **`there is no package called 'ratdat'`** (or `tidyverse`). Install it by running `install.packages(c("tidyverse", "ratdat"))` in the Console. Don't put `install.packages()` in your document.
- **`object 'complete_old' not found`.** The `ratdat` package hasn't been loaded. Run the Task 1 chunk first.
- **`could not find function "..."`.** The name is misspelled, or the code uses a package that isn't loaded. Compare the name with the lesson.
- **`object '...' not found` while drawing a plot.** The assistant used a column name that isn't in your data. Compare it with `names(complete_old)`, and ask for a corrected version.
- **The code reads a file, such as `read_csv("data/surveys.csv")`.** The data come with the `ratdat` package, so no file is needed. Tell the assistant to use `complete_old`, and ask for a new version.
- **A warning such as `Removed 3081 rows containing missing values`.** This is a warning, not an error: the plot was still drawn. Check 3 in Part 3 asks you to explain the number.
- **The code uses functions you haven't met, such as `filter()` or `%>%`.** That is what Check 4 is for. You can ask the assistant to rewrite the code without them, but note that you did.

Facts about complete_old for checking students' claims: 16,878 rows and 13 columns, with class tbl_df, tbl, and data.frame. Year runs from 1977 to 1989. Weight has 1,692 missing values and hindfoot_length has 2,733, and 3,081 rows are missing at least one of the two, which is the number in the warning on the first two scatterplots. The boxplot warnings give 2,733. The minimum weight is NA until na.rm = TRUE is used, and then it is 4. The 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles of weight are 24, 42, and 53, and those of hindfoot_length are 21, 35, and 37. The sex column holds F, M, and 1,300 blank entries (empty strings, not NA), so the factor has three levels, the faceted plot has three panels, and coloring by sex gives a legend with three entries, one of them blank. There are five plot types. The wording of warnings varies a little with the version of ggplot2.

In the prompts, look for the four parts from step 2 (who the student is and what they are using; the data, with the data frame, no file needed, and the column names; the tasks; and what to use and what to return), and for follow-ups that include the exact error message and the code that caused it.

Things worth looking for in submissions: code that reads a file instead of using complete_old; invented column names; pipes or filter() despite the constraint; extra packages; and a Check 4 that says None without saying how the student checked.

## Week 11: Wrangling Data with dplyr and tidyr

This week, you'll practice `select()`, `filter()`, the pipe, `group_by()` with `summarize()`, and `pivot_wider()` and `pivot_longer()`, using the `complete_old` data from the Data Carpentry lesson.

### The data

Load the packages, and the data are ready to use as a data frame called `complete_old`:

```
library(tidyverse)
library(ratdat)
```

The lesson reads the same data from a CSV file into an object called `surveys`. We use `complete_old` instead, so your numbers should match the lesson's, with one difference that you'll find in Part 2.

### Questions

Answer each question with R code. Use the object names given, and work in order, because later questions use the objects you make in earlier ones. Each question ends with a check, a value your result should match. If yours doesn't, find out why, rather than changing your answer to fit the number. Use only the functions from the lesson so far: `select()`, `filter()`, `group_by()`, `summarize()`, `arrange()`, `desc()`, `ungroup()`, `pivot_wider()`, `pivot_longer()`, the pipe `%>%`, and `ggplot2` functions.

**Part 1: Select, filter, and pipes**

**Question 1.** Select the columns `year`, `month`, `species_id`, and `plot_id`, in that order.

*Check:* Your result has 16,878 rows and 4 columns, and its first row is 1977, 7, NL, 2.

**Question 2.** Keep only the rows where `species_id` is `DM` or `DO`, and where `weight` isn't missing.

*Check:* Your result has 6,909 rows.

**Question 3.** Using a single pipeline, keep the rows from 1988 where `hindfoot_length` isn't missing, and then keep only the columns `record_id`, `species_id`, and `hindfoot_length`. Save the result as `hindfoot_1988`. Think about the order of the two steps: the filter uses a column that the select removes.

*Check:* Your result has 1,332 rows and 3 columns.

**Part 2: Split-apply-combine**

**Question 4.** For each value of `sex`, how many animals are there, and what is their mean weight? Ignore missing weights when you calculate the mean.

*Check:* F has 7,318 animals with a mean weight of 53.1, and M has 8,260 animals with a mean weight of 53.2.

**Question 5.** Look at the groups in your answer to Question 4. One of them isn't F or M. Which group is it, and how many rows are in it? Try to remove it from the data with `filter(!is.na(sex))`. How many rows are left, and why? Then write a filter that does remove it. Write your answers as comments.

*Check:* After your corrected filter, 15,578 rows should remain.

**Question 6.** For each `species_id`, calculate the mean weight and the number of animals, using only animals that have a recorded weight. Sort the result from the heaviest mean weight to the lightest.

*Check:* Your result has 18 rows. The first row is NL, with a mean weight of 158.4 and 824 animals, and the last is BA, with a mean weight of 7.0 and 3 animals.

**Part 3: Pivoting**

**Question 7.** Using only animals with a recorded weight from the species `DM`, `DO`, `DS`, and `NL`, calculate the mean weight of each species in each year. The result should have just three columns, `year`, `species_id`, and `mean_weight`, with no groups left over. Save it as `weight_by_species_year`.

*Check:* Your result has 51 rows and 3 columns. In 1977, the mean weight of DM was 41.1.

**Question 8.** Use `pivot_wider()` to reshape `weight_by_species_year` into a table with one row for each year and one column for each species. Save it as `weight_wide`. One cell of the result is a missing value. Which species and year is it, and what does it mean? Write your answer as a comment.

*Check:* Your result has 13 rows and 5 columns (`year`, `DM`, `DO`, `DS`, and `NL`), and contains exactly 1 missing value.

**Question 9.** Use `pivot_longer()` to reshape `weight_wide` back into long format, with the columns `year`, `species_id`, and `mean_weight`. Remove the rows with a missing value. Save it as `weight_long`.

*Check:* Your result has 51 rows and 3 columns, the same number of rows as `weight_by_species_year`.

**Question 10.** Using `weight_long`, make a line plot with year on the x axis, mean weight on the y axis, and one colored line for each species. Add a title, and axis labels that include the units (weight is in grams). Then, as a comment, say why `ggplot2` needs the long format for this plot rather than the wide one.

*Check:* Your plot has four lines, and one of them starts a year later than the others.

### What to submit

Submit your R script to Canvas. Put your answers to the written questions (5, 8, and 10) in comments next to your code. You may use an AI assistant, as in Week 10, but you must be able to explain every line you hand in, and if you used one, say how at the end of your script in a comment.

INSTRUCTOR NOTES (not visible in rendered output)

Solutions and grading notes. The numbers each question should produce are in the check lines above.

library(tidyverse)
library(ratdat)

# Question 1
q1 <- select(complete_old, year, month, species_id, plot_id)

# Question 2
q2 <- complete_old %>%
  filter(species_id %in% c("DM", "DO") & !is.na(weight))

# Question 3
hindfoot_1988 <- complete_old %>%
  filter(year == 1988 & !is.na(hindfoot_length)) %>%
  select(record_id, species_id, hindfoot_length)

# Question 4
by_sex <- complete_old %>%
  group_by(sex) %>%
  summarize(mean_weight = mean(weight, na.rm = TRUE),
            n = n())

# Question 5
# The odd group is the rows where sex is blank (an empty string), 1,300 of them.
# filter(!is.na(sex)) leaves all 16,878 rows, because a blank string is not NA.
# In the lesson, the surveys object comes from read_csv, which turns blanks into NA,
# so there the group shows up as NA; complete_old keeps them as empty strings.
q5_wrong <- complete_old %>% filter(!is.na(sex))
q5 <- complete_old %>% filter(sex %in% c("F", "M"))

# Question 6
by_species <- complete_old %>%
  filter(!is.na(weight)) %>%
  group_by(species_id) %>%
  summarize(mean_weight = mean(weight),
            n = n()) %>%
  arrange(desc(mean_weight))

# Question 7
weight_by_species_year <- complete_old %>%
  filter(!is.na(weight) & species_id %in% c("DM", "DO", "DS", "NL")) %>%
  group_by(year, species_id) %>%
  summarize(mean_weight = mean(weight)) %>%
  ungroup()

# Question 8
# The missing cell is NL in 1977: no NL with a recorded weight was captured that year,
# either because none were caught or because none were weighed.
weight_wide <- weight_by_species_year %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = species_id, values_from = mean_weight)

# Question 9
weight_long <- weight_wide %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -year, names_to = "species_id", values_to = "mean_weight") %>%
  filter(!is.na(mean_weight))

# Question 10
q10 <- ggplot(data = weight_long, mapping = aes(x = year, y = mean_weight, color = species_id)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "Mean weight of four rodent species by year",
       x = "Year",
       y = "Mean weight (g)")
q10

# ggplot2 maps one variable to each aesthetic, so species has to be a single column for it
# to be mapped to color. In the wide table each species is its own column.
